nodes.label: Exponential Functions, Real Exponents, and Multiplicative Change
nodes.explanation: Assumes secondary entry background in integer and rational exponent laws (b⁰ = 1, b⁻ⁿ = 1/bⁿ, b^(p/q) = (q-th root of b)^p, bʳbˢ = b^(r+s), (bʳ)ˢ = b^(rs)) and general function language (domain, range, graphs, monotonicity, asymptotes, transformations, and inverses) from recommended preparation in Radicals and Rational Exponents and Function Language and Transformations. Develops exponential functions f(x) = a·bˣ (b > 0, b ≠ 1, a ≠ 0), explaining why b > 0 is needed for real-valued outputs and why b = 1 degenerates to a constant function, while explicitly supplying the continuous monotonic extension of bˣ from rational to irrational real exponents (leaving formal construction to Real Analysis). Contrasts exponential multiplicative change (constant ratio f(x + 1)/f(x) = b per unit step) with linear additive change (constant difference), establishes parent graph features for growth (b > 1) versus decay (0 < b < 1)—domain ℝ, range (0, ∞) for a > 0, y-intercept (0, a), horizontal asymptote y = 0, and strict monotonicity (hence injectivity)—and trains determining a·bˣ from a table or any two points. Enables the learner to identify exponential relationships, graph basic growth and decay functions, and construct exact formulas a·bˣ from two data points. Leaves transformations, Euler's number e, and logarithms to subsequent branches.

nodes.label: Transformations of Exponential Graphs
nodes.explanation: Builds on exponential functions and applies general function transformation rules (assumed from recommended preparation in Function Language and Transformations) to analyze and sketch f(x) = a·b^(k(x - h)) + c. Anchors every sketch on the horizontal asymptote y = c and two reference points, tracking how vertical shifts set the asymptote and range ((c, ∞) if a > 0, (-∞, c) if a < 0), how reflections across the y-axis invert the base via b^(-x) = (1/b)ˣ (converting growth into decay and vice versa), and how horizontal shifts behave algebraically as vertical scalings via b^(x - h) = b^(-h)·bˣ (explaining why a shifted exponential can always be rewritten without an explicit horizontal shift). Trains reconstructing a formula of the form a·bˣ + c from a graph displaying a horizontal asymptote and two points, and diagnosing growth vs. decay when both a and k may be negative. Enables the learner to sketch transformed exponential graphs accurately, read off domains, ranges, intercepts, and asymptotes, and write formulas from transformed graphs.

nodes.label: Compound Interest, Effective Rates, and the Natural Base e
nodes.explanation: Builds on exponential functions to model discrete periodic compounding and motivate Euler's number e and the natural exponential function eˣ. Derives the compound-interest formula A(t) = P(1 + r/n)^(nt) from repeated multiplicative growth by factor (1 + r/n) per period, introduces the effective annual yield (APY) r_eff = (1 + r/n)ⁿ - 1 to compare nominal rates across different compounding frequencies, and examines the behavior of (1 + 1/n)ⁿ as n grows large—explicitly supplying without formal ε-N proof that (1 + 1/n)ⁿ converges to the irrational constant e ≈ 2.71828... and that (1 + r/n)^(nt) approaches P·e^(rt) under continuous compounding. Establishes the graph and properties of f(x) = eˣ (strictly increasing, domain ℝ, range (0, ∞), horizontal asymptote y = 0, lying between 2ˣ and 3ˣ) and compares discrete versus continuous growth models. Leaves solving for elapsed time t and converting general bases bˣ into e^(kx) until the natural logarithm ln is introduced in a subsequent synthesis lesson.

nodes.label: Logarithms as Inverses of Exponential Functions
nodes.explanation: Builds on the strict monotonicity (one-to-one property) of bˣ and applies inverse-function concepts from recommended preparation (Function Language and Transformations) to define logarithms for any valid base b > 0, b ≠ 1. Establishes the defining equivalence y = log_b(x) ⇔ bʸ = x for x > 0, emphasizing that a logarithm is an exponent, and introduces the common logarithm log(x) = log₁₀(x) (leaving the natural logarithm ln(x) = log_e(x) for the later synthesis with base e). Develops exact evaluation of logarithms using rational and negative exponents (such as log₂(1/8) = -3, log₉(3) = 1/2, log_b(1) = 0, log_b(b) = 1), the inverse cancellation identities log_b(bˣ) = x (for all x ∈ ℝ) and b^(log_b x) = x (for x > 0), domain determination for logarithmic expressions (requiring strictly positive arguments), and the parent graph of y = log_b(x) obtained by reflecting y = bˣ across y = x (domain (0, ∞), range ℝ, vertical asymptote x = 0, x-intercept (1, 0), increasing for b > 1 and decreasing for 0 < b < 1). Enables the learner to convert fluently between exponential and logarithmic forms, evaluate exact logarithms, find logarithmic domains, and sketch parent logarithmic graphs.

nodes.label: Transformations and Domains of Logarithmic Graphs
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes exponential graph transformations with logarithms as inverses to analyze and graph g(x) = a·log_b(k(x - h)) + c for general bases b > 0, b ≠ 1. Anchors every graph on its exact domain k(x - h) > 0 and vertical asymptote x = h (highlighting why horizontal shifts—not vertical shifts—move the asymptote of a logarithm, in exact mirror symmetry with exponentials), and tracks how reflections across the y-axis flip the domain to (-∞, h) while reflections across the x-axis correspond to inverting the base via -log_b(x) = log_(1/b)(x). Computes exact algebraic inverses of transformed exponentials y = a·b^(k(x - h)) + c and transformed logarithms y = a·log_b(k(x - h)) + c, verifying that the horizontal asymptote y = c of one swaps directly with the vertical asymptote x = c of the other. Enables the learner to sketch transformed logarithmic graphs with accurate asymptotes and anchor points, read domains and ranges, and pair transformed exponential and logarithmic functions as explicit inverses.

nodes.label: Algebraic Laws of Logarithms and Change of Base
nodes.explanation: Builds on the inverse definition of logarithms for general bases b > 0, b ≠ 1 to derive and apply the algebraic laws of logarithms. Proves the product rule log_b(MN) = log_b(M) + log_b(N), quotient rule log_b(M/N) = log_b(M) - log_b(N), and power rule log_b(Mᵖ) = p·log_b(M) directly from the corresponding exponent laws by setting M = bᵘ and N = bᵛ (for M, N > 0), and derives the change-of-base formula log_b(x) = log_c(x)/log_c(b) together with key corollaries log_b(a) = 1/log_a(b) and log_(b^k)(x) = (1/k)log_b(x). Trains expanding single logarithms and condensing sums/differences while explicitly targeting two persistent traps: illegal linear distribution (log(A + B) ≠ log A + log B and log(A)/log(B) ≠ log(A - B)) and silent domain alteration when applying rules (specifically log_b(x²) = 2·log_b|x| rather than 2·log_b(x) on negative x, and why log_b(x) + log_b(x - 1) has domain x > 1 whereas log_b(x(x - 1)) also admits x < 0). Enables the learner to derive, simplify, expand, condense, and rebase logarithmic expressions while preserving exact domain validity.

nodes.label: Natural Logarithms and Solving Exponential Equations
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes the natural base e with the laws of logarithms and change of base to introduce the natural logarithm ln(x) = log_e(x) and master solving exponential equations. Establishes the natural inverse identities ln(eˣ) = x, e^(ln x) = x (x > 0), and the universal base-conversion bridge bˣ = e^(x ln b) (so every exponential function is a horizontally scaled natural exponential). Develops all five core algebraic strategies for exponential equations: (1) matching a common base (4^(x+1) = 8^(2x-3)); (2) isolating the exponential term and applying ln or log_b (5·3^(2x-1) = 20, diagnosing no real solution when the isolated exponential equals a non-positive number); (3) taking ln of both sides when distinct bases carry variable exponents (2^(x+1) = 5^(2x-3)) and collecting linear x-terms; (4) factoring out a common exponential factor (3^(x+2) - 3ˣ = 72); and (5) quadratic substitution u = bˣ > 0 (e^(2x) - 5eˣ + 6 = 0 or 4ˣ - 3·2ˣ - 4 = 0, discarding any root u ≤ 0). Emphasizes producing exact symbolic solutions in terms of ln or log before optional decimal approximations. Enables the learner to choose and execute the cleanest method for arbitrary precalculus exponential equations.

nodes.label: Solving Logarithmic Equations and Domain Verification
nodes.explanation: Builds on natural logarithms and exponential equation solving (and uses logarithm laws and change of base from earlier ancestors) to develop complete methods for solving logarithmic equations while rigorously eliminating extraneous roots. Covers the primary equation classes: one-to-one matching log_b(A(x)) = log_b(B(x)) ⇒ A(x) = B(x); condensing sums and differences before converting log_b(A(x)) = c into A(x) = bᶜ (including natural-log equations yielding eᶜ); mixed-base equations resolved via change of base (such as log₂(x) + log₄(x) = 6); quadratic-in-logarithm substitutions u = log_b(x) (such as (ln x)² - 3 ln x + 2 = 0, noting that u may be negative here unlike u = bˣ!); and variable-exponent equations solved by taking logarithms of both sides (such as x^(ln x) = e⁴ for x > 0). Uses domain widening under log_b(A) + log_b(B) → log_b(AB) as the central conceptual reason why algebraically valid steps can manufacture extraneous solutions, making verification of every candidate against the original equation's argument positivity (and base positivity/non-unity when the base contains x) mandatory. Enables the learner to solve single-base, mixed-base, and quadratic logarithmic equations cleanly without retaining invalid roots.

nodes.label: Exponential and Logarithmic Inequalities
nodes.explanation: Builds on exponential and logarithmic equation solving (assuming familiarity with linear and simple quadratic inequalities from secondary algebra) to solve inequalities involving exponentials and logarithms. Establishes monotonicity as the governing principle: applying or undoing bˣ or log_b(x) preserves inequality direction when b > 1 and reverses direction when 0 < b < 1. Develops complete workflows for exponential inequalities—common-base comparison (1/3)^(x-1) > 9, taking ln of both sides when bases differ, and quadratic-in-bˣ inequalities such as 2^(2x) - 5·2ˣ + 4 < 0—and logarithmic inequalities such as log_(1/2)(x - 1) + log_(1/2)(x - 3) ≥ -3 and log₂(x + 2) < log₂(3x - 1). Emphasizes intersecting every algebraic solution interval with the original logarithmic domain restrictions (argument > 0) and guarding carefully against multiplying by ln(b) < 0 when 0 < b < 1. Enables the learner to solve exponential and logarithmic inequalities accurately in interval notation across both b > 1 and 0 < b < 1 regimes.

nodes.label: Exponential Growth, Decay, Doubling Time, and Half-Life Models
nodes.explanation: Builds on natural logarithms and exponential equation solving to construct, convert, and solve unconstrained exponential growth and decay models in finance, biology, chemistry, and physics. Connects the discrete-rate form A(t) = A₀(1 + r)ᵗ, the continuous-rate form A(t) = A₀e^(kt), and the doubling-time / half-life forms A₀·2^(t/T_d) and A₀·(1/2)^(t/T_(1/2)) via the exact conversion identities k = ln(1 + r), T_d = (ln 2)/k, and T_(1/2) = -(ln 2)/k (for k < 0). Trains calibrating the rate parameter k from two measurements (or from a percentage change over an arbitrary time span), solving for elapsed time t via ln (such as radiocarbon dating, compound-interest time-to-target, or drug clearance below a threshold), and comparing models stated in different rate conventions. Explicitly emphasizes that doubling time and half-life are independent of the initial amount A₀—a defining structural signature of exponential processes. Enables the learner to formulate, convert, calibrate, and interpret exponential growth and decay models cleanly.

nodes.label: Shifted Exponential (Newton's Cooling) and Logistic Growth Models
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes exponential graph transformations with continuous exponential growth/decay modeling to analyze bounded processes whose long-term behavior approaches a nonzero equilibrium. Develops shifted exponential models T(t) = T_env + (T₀ - T_env)e^(-kt) (Newton's Law of Cooling and Warming, as well as bounded saturation models y(t) = L - (L - y₀)e^(-kt)), interpreting the ambient temperature or ceiling L directly as the horizontal asymptote from exponential transformations, solving for the decay constant k from one intermediate observation, and finding the time to reach a target value. Introduces the logistic growth model P(t) = L / (1 + A·e^(-kt)) (explicitly supplying the formula without differential equations), analyzing its carrying capacity L (upper horizontal asymptote as t → ∞), initial population P(0) = L/(1 + A), transition from near-exponential early growth to bounded saturation, and the half-capacity point P = L/2 occurring at t = (ln A)/k (qualitatively described as the point of fastest growth, leaving derivative verification to calculus), plus calibrating A and k from data given L and solving algebraically for t. Enables the learner to build, calibrate, sketch, and solve shifted-exponential and logistic models in applied contexts.

nodes.label: Logarithmic Scales: Decibels, pH, and Magnitude Ratios
nodes.explanation: Builds on the laws of logarithms and base-10 common logarithms (without requiring base e or natural logarithms) to interpret and compute with scientific logarithmic scales that compress wide multiplicative ranges into additive steps. Develops work with acidity pH = -log₁₀[H⁺], sound intensity level β = 10·log₁₀(I/I₀) in decibels, and seismic magnitude M = log₁₀(I/I₀), using quotient and power laws of logarithms as the central bridge to translate additive scale differences ΔL directly into multiplicative intensity ratios (for example, ΔM = 1.6 corresponds to intensity ratio 10^(1.6) ≈ 39.8, and Δβ = +3 dB corresponds to roughly doubling intensity). Directly addresses the major misconception of treating logarithmic measurements additively when combining independent physical sources (showing why two identical 70 dB machines produce 70 + 10·log₁₀(2) ≈ 73 dB rather than 140 dB) and trains inverting scale readings back to physical concentrations or intensities. Enables the learner to compare orders of magnitude, convert fluently between logarithmic scale differences and physical ratios, and combine physical sources correctly.

nodes.label: Semi-Log and Log-Log Plots for Model Identification
nodes.explanation: Optional enrichment building on natural logarithms and logarithm laws (and basic linear equations y = mx + b) to diagnose and fit nonlinear relationships by transforming axes logarithmically. Establishes the exact linearization bridges: an exponential relationship y = a·bˣ becomes linear on a semi-log plot via ln(y) = (ln b)x + ln(a) (equivalently log₁₀(y) = (log₁₀ b)x + log₁₀(a)), whereas a power-law relationship y = a·xᵖ (for x > 0) becomes linear on a log-log plot via ln(y) = p·ln(x) + ln(a). Trains inspecting tables or plots of (x, ln y) versus (ln x, ln y) to distinguish exponential growth from power-law scaling, extracting the slope and vertical intercept of the linearized line, and back-transforming accurately to recover a = e^(intercept) and either b = e^(slope) or p = slope—explicitly guarding against the common error of reading the intercept directly as a rather than ln(a). Enables the learner to identify exponential versus power-law models from data and recover exact model parameters using semi-log and log-log transformations.

nodes.label: Hyperbolic Functions and Their Logarithmic Inverses
nodes.explanation: Optional enrichment synthesizing exponential graph transformations with natural logarithms and quadratic exponential equations to introduce the hyperbolic functions purely algebraically from eˣ and e⁻ˣ. Defines cosh(x) = (eˣ + e⁻ˣ)/2, sinh(x) = (eˣ - e⁻ˣ)/2, and tanh(x) = sinh(x)/cosh(x) = (eˣ - e⁻ˣ)/(eˣ + e⁻ˣ), establishing their even/odd symmetries, exact ranges, and graphs (noting that cosh(x) ≥ 1 with minimum (0, 1), sinh(x) is strictly increasing onto ℝ, and tanh(x) is strictly increasing onto (-1, 1) with horizontal asymptotes y = ±1). Proves core algebraic identities—cosh²(x) - sinh²(x) = 1, 1 - tanh²(x) = sech²(x), and the addition/double-argument identities—directly from exponent laws, and derives explicit logarithmic formulas for inverse hyperbolic functions: arsinh(x) = ln(x + √(x² + 1)), arcosh(x) = ln(x + √(x² - 1)) for x ≥ 1 (restricting cosh to y ≥ 0), and artanh(x) = (1/2)ln((1 + x)/(1 - x)) for |x| < 1 by solving quadratic equations in eʸ. Leaves calculus derivatives, integrals, and catenary differential equations to calculus.
